Source: https://samarthfire.in/housing-society-fire-safety-checklist
Title: Housing Society Fire Safety Checklist for Committee Members
Last updated: 2026-11-04

A housing society committee can use this checklist to identify visible issues and organise follow-up work. It is not a statutory audit form and cannot replace inspection by a competent fire safety professional.




## 1. Keep escape routes clear



- Keep staircases, corridors, exit doors and final exits free from storage and obstructions. 

- Do not lock or block fire exits in a way that prevents safe escape. 

- Check that fire doors close properly and are not wedged open. 

- Keep access for fire service vehicles and emergency responders clear. 

- Check that exit signs and emergency lights appear intact and arrange testing under the maintenance plan. 







## 2. Check the fire safety equipment

Make a list of the equipment installed in the building. Depending on the approved plan, this may include fire pumps, hydrants, wet risers, landing valves, hose reels, sprinklers, extinguishers, fire alarm panels, detectors and manual call points. Check that the equipment is visible, accessible and not obviously damaged. Keep service and test records.






## 3. Review the pump room and water supply

Keep the pump room locked against unauthorised access but available to responsible personnel and emergency responders. Do not use it for storage. Review the pump and tank records, controller indications, visible leakage and any faults reported by the maintenance provider. Functional tests should be planned and carried out by competent personnel.






## 4. Check fire extinguishers

Confirm extinguishers are in their assigned locations, easy to reach, correctly identified and visibly in serviceable condition. Check their inspection tags and service records. The correct type and number depend on the risks and layout of the building; do not assume one extinguisher type is suitable for every area.






## 5. Look at everyday housekeeping and risks



- Do not store combustible materials in staircases, lift lobbies, electrical rooms or pump rooms. 

- Keep electrical panels accessible and report damaged wiring, burning smells or unusual heating. 

- Manage hot work, temporary electrical work, waste and gas storage through a responsible process. 

- Keep parking areas, fire access routes and equipment cabinets free from obstructions. 







## 6. Prepare residents, guards and staff

Make sure people know how to raise the alarm, which exits to use, where the assembly point is and whom to contact. Agree how assistance will be arranged for older residents, children and people who may need help using stairs. Train security staff to report faults and follow the building’s emergency plan rather than improvise repairs.






## 7. Keep the records together

Keep the approved fire plan, equipment list, AMC/work orders, pump and system test reports, extinguisher service tags, fault register, drill records and statutory documents in one place. Give the committee and facility manager a way to see which defects are still open.






## 8. Turn the checklist into action

For each problem, record the location, the risk, who will arrange the fix and by when. Prioritise anything that could affect escape or stop an installed life-safety system from working. Arrange repairs and testing through a competent provider.






## Important note

Use the current Maharashtra fire-safety rules, the building’s approved fire plan and the competent authority’s directions for statutory requirements. The Maharashtra Fire & Emergency Services official website publishes the Act and amended Rules.

Title: Workplace Fire Safety, First Aid & CPR Training: What to Expect
Last updated: 2026-11-04

Training should match the workplace and the people taking part. A warehouse, office, school and housing society do not have the same layout or emergency arrangements. Plan the session around the site’s actual risks and approved emergency plan.




## Fire safety awareness

Participants can learn how to recognise common fire hazards, raise the alarm, report a problem, follow exit signs, use the designated escape routes and reach the assembly point. Explain who coordinates the response and how visitors or contractors are included.






## Fire extinguisher and equipment demonstrations

A supervised demonstration can help participants understand extinguisher labels, fire classes, operating instructions and safe handling. Practical use should only take place in a controlled exercise, with suitable equipment, a safe location and competent supervision. It should never encourage people to fight a fire instead of evacuating.






## Evacuation drills and team roles

A drill can help test whether the alarm can be heard, the routes are clear, wardens understand their roles and people know where to assemble. Record the lessons and assign actions to address blocked routes, unclear instructions or other gaps.






## First aid and CPR training

First aid and CPR sessions introduce participants to basic emergency response and practical skills under instructor supervision. The topics, depth and certificate (where applicable) depend on the course and training provider. Confirm the course outline, instructor credentials, assessment and certificate details before booking.






## How should an organisation prepare?



- Share the site layout, emergency plan and type of premises. 

- Estimate the number and roles of participants. 

- Identify language, accessibility or mobility needs. 

- Agree the training topics and whether practical demonstrations are included. 

- Choose a safe space and coordinate with the facility/security team. 

- Keep attendance and post-session action records. 







## Important note

Training is not a substitute for an approved emergency plan, working equipment or emergency services. In a real incident, raise the alarm, evacuate when required and contact emergency responders.

Source: https://samarthfire.in/workplace-first-aid-cpr-training-guide
Title: Workplace First Aid and CPR Training: What Should a Session Cover?
Last updated: 2026-11-04

First aid and CPR awareness can help staff and residents respond calmly while professional medical help is on the way. It is not a substitute for emergency medical care, and people should follow the training they receive from qualified instructors and the local emergency response procedure.



## Start with the people and the workplace

Identify who will attend, the type of workplace, the number of participants, language needs and any known hazards. A school, office, warehouse, housing society and industrial site may need different examples and practical activities.



## Topics to discuss with the training provider



- How to recognise an emergency and call for professional help. 

- How to make the area safe before approaching an injured person. 

- How to respond when a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, within the limits of the course and the learner’s training. 

- CPR practice using suitable training equipment where included in the course. 

- Basic first aid topics relevant to the site, such as bleeding, burns or choking, taught by a competent instructor. 

- How first aid arrangements connect with the site’s emergency contact and incident-reporting process. 




## Make the session practical and accessible

Ask how much of the session is demonstration and supervised practice, what equipment is provided, how many people can practise at once, and whether the content can be adapted for the audience. Arrange clear space, suitable seating and reasonable access for participants.



## Ask about the certificate before booking

Training certificates can differ by provider, course and instructor qualification. Before advertising a session as accredited or certified, ask who conducts it, what syllabus is followed, what assessment is included and which organisation issues the certificate. Do not assume every awareness session gives the same qualification.



## Connect first aid with fire safety

First aid sessions can be planned alongside fire safety awareness, extinguisher demonstrations and evacuation drills. Keep each activity controlled, supervised and suited to the building’s emergency plan. A practical demonstration does not replace regular system maintenance or a site-specific evacuation procedure.



## Plan the follow-up

Keep attendance records, training topics, trainer details, completion documents and any follow-up actions. Review the programme when the workforce, site hazards or emergency arrangements change.

Source: https://samarthfire.in/building-evacuation-plan-guide
Title: Building Evacuation Plan: 6 Steps Every Housing Society Should Know
Last updated: 2026-11-02

Evacuation plans fail when they are too complicated to remember under stress. These six steps cover the sequence that matters most — and each links to where you can go deeper.




## 1. Raise the alarm

Activate the nearest manual call point if one is available, shout to alert neighbours, and call the fire brigade on 101 (or 112 ) immediately — don't assume someone else already has.






## 2. Floor wardens act

Trained wardens sweep their assigned floor, direct people to the nearest safe exit, and close doors behind them as they leave — closed doors slow fire and smoke spread significantly.






## 3. Use the stairs — never lifts

Walk, don't run, to the nearest stairwell. Lifts can lose power or open directly onto a fire floor, and must never be used during an evacuation.






## 4. Go to the assembly point

The designated muster point should be clearly marked, known in advance by every resident or staff member, and positioned clear of building exits and the fire brigade's access route.






## 5. Take a headcount

Each warden confirms everyone from their floor or department is present at the assembly point, and reports any missing person to the fire brigade immediately on arrival — this single step is often what finds someone in time.






## 6. Brief the fire brigade

When the fire brigade arrives, someone familiar with the building should be ready to share the fire's location, any known hazards (gas cylinders, chemical storage), and where hydrants and risers are located.






## A plan only works if it's practised

Wardens should be nominated and trained in advance, and the sequence rehearsed through regular drills — see our housing society fire drill guide for how to plan one.

Source: https://samarthfire.in/conventional-vs-addressable-fire-alarm
Title: Conventional vs Addressable Fire Alarm Systems: Key Differences
Last updated: 2026-11-02

Both conventional and addressable fire alarm systems do the same core job — detect smoke or heat and raise an alarm. They differ in how much detail the control panel gives your team when it does.




## Conventional systems: zone-level detection

Conventional panels divide the building into wired zones — typically by floor or area. When any detector in a zone triggers, the panel shows which zone is in alarm, but not which exact detector. Someone still has to walk the zone to find the source. This works well for smaller buildings, shops and simple single-floor layouts where "zone 3" already tells the team roughly where to look.






## Addressable systems: device-level detection

Addressable panels assign a unique digital address to every detector, call point and sounder on the loop. When one triggers, the panel displays the exact device — for example "Floor 3, Corridor B, Detector 07" — cutting the time it takes to locate and confirm the fire. This precision is why addressable systems are standard in multi-storey, large-footprint or high-occupancy buildings.






## Side-by-side comparison


| Conventional | Addressable |


Fault/fire location | Zone-level only | Exact device |

Wiring | Parallel zone circuits | Loop wiring, fewer cable runs on large sites |

Best suited to | Small / simple buildings | High-rise, large or complex buildings |

Upfront cost | Generally lower | Generally higher, offset by easier diagnostics |

Expansion | Limited by zone wiring | Devices added along the loop more flexibly |









## What actually decides which you need

Building height, floor area, occupancy type and the applicable fire code — not personal preference — determine the system class required. A fire safety assessment confirms what your specific building needs and whether an existing conventional system still meets current requirements.






## Frequently asked questions



### Can a conventional system be upgraded to addressable later?
Usually not as a simple add-on. Addressable systems use different detectors, wiring topology (a loop rather than parallel zone wiring) and a different panel, so an upgrade is normally a planned replacement rather than a retrofit of individual parts.



### Which system is required by law in Maharashtra?
The applicable building and fire code, building height, occupancy and the approved fire plan determine what is required for a specific building — not a blanket rule. Confirm the requirement for your building with a licensed fire agency or the Directorate of Maharashtra Fire & Emergency Services.


---

Source: https://samarthfire.in/fire-extinguisher-types-guide
Title: Fire Extinguisher Types Explained: A, B, C, D & F/K Classes
Last updated: 2026-11-02

Fire extinguishers are not interchangeable. Each type is designed, pressurised and labelled for specific fuel types — using the wrong one on a liquid fire or live electrical equipment can spread the fire or create a shock hazard. Knowing the five fire classes used in India is the fastest way to choose correctly.




## The five fire classes


Class | Typical fuel | Suitable extinguisher |


A | Wood, paper, cloth, most plastics | Water, foam, or ABC dry powder |

B | Petrol, diesel, paint, solvents, oil | Foam, ABC dry powder, or CO₂ |

C | Flammable gases — LPG, PNG, methane | ABC dry powder, after isolating the gas supply |

D | Combustible metals — magnesium, aluminium swarf, sodium | Specialist metal-fire powder only |

F / K | Cooking oils and fats | Wet chemical extinguisher |




Most Indian homes, offices and common areas are protected mainly against Class A, B and electrical risk, which is why the general-purpose ABC dry powder and CO₂ extinguishers are so common. Class D and specialised Class F/K risks are usually confined to specific areas — a workshop, a commercial kitchen — and are addressed separately in the fire plan.






## Water and foam extinguishers

Water extinguishers cool burning solids (Class A) effectively but must never be used on burning liquids, live electrical equipment or cooking oil — the stream can spread a liquid fire or create a severe shock risk. Foam extinguishers add a smothering layer on top of flammable liquids and also work on Class A fires, which is why foam is common in car parks, generator rooms and fuel-storage areas.






## CO₂ extinguishers

CO₂ (carbon dioxide) extinguishers displace oxygen and leave no residue, which makes them the preferred choice around electrical panels, server rooms, control rooms and sensitive equipment. They are less effective outdoors or in draughty areas, and the discharge horn gets extremely cold — hold it by the handle, not the horn.






## ABC dry powder extinguishers

ABC dry powder is the most common general-purpose extinguisher in Indian buildings because it covers solids, liquids and (with the gas supply isolated) gas fires in one cylinder. The trade-off is residue: the fine powder is corrosive to electronics and leaves a mess that needs cleaning, so many sites still prefer CO₂ specifically near computers and panels.






## Wet chemical extinguishers (kitchens)

Commercial kitchens with deep-fat fryers need a wet chemical extinguisher. It applies a fine mist that cools the oil and forms a soap-like layer (saponification) that seals the surface and prevents re-ignition — something water, foam, CO₂ and dry powder cannot safely do on hot oil.






## Common mistakes that make an extinguisher useless



- Wrong type for the fuel — e.g. water on an electrical or oil fire. 

- Expired or unpressurised cylinder — the gauge needle should sit in the green zone. 

- Blocked access — extinguishers stacked behind furniture or stock. 

- Seized pin or seal — never tested, so it fails exactly when needed. 

- No one trained in the P.A.S.S. technique (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep). 







## Frequently asked questions



### Can I use a CO2 extinguisher on a cooking oil fire?
No. Cooking oil and fat fires (Class F/K) need a wet chemical extinguisher. CO2 and dry powder can disturb hot oil and are not designed to cool or seal it, so they are not suitable for deep-fat fryer fires.



### Is one ABC dry powder extinguisher enough for a whole flat or office?
The right number, size and placement of extinguishers depends on floor area, occupancy and travel distance under the applicable building and fire code, not a fixed rule of thumb. A site assessment by a licensed agency gives a specific recommendation.


---

Source: https://samarthfire.in/wet-riser-hydrant-system-guide
Title: Wet Riser Hydrant System Explained: How Building Fire Water Works
Last updated: 2026-11-02

A wet riser system keeps a vertical pipe permanently filled with pressurised water so that firefighters — or trained residents, where permitted — can connect a hose on any floor without waiting for water to travel up from the ground. Here is how the pieces fit together, from the tank to the hose.




## 1. The underground static tank

A dedicated fire-water reserve, sized to the building's design requirement, is kept separate from domestic water. This is the supply the pumps draw from during a fire, independent of the municipal connection.






## 2. The pump room: main, standby and jockey

Three pumps work together. The main pump (usually electric) provides the primary flow and pressure. A standby pump (often diesel) takes over automatically if the electric supply fails — exactly when a fire is most likely to have also tripped the power. A small jockey pump runs continuously in the background, topping up minor pressure loss so the main pumps don't cycle on and off unnecessarily.






## 3. The riser pipe — always full, always pressurised

Unlike a dry riser (filled only when the fire brigade pumps into it), a wet riser stays permanently charged with water under pressure. That means a hose can be connected and used within seconds on any floor, without waiting for the pumps to fill an empty pipe first.






## 4. Landing valves and hose cabinets on every floor

At each floor, a landing valve taps into the riser, feeding a hose reel or hose cabinet. These must stay accessible and visibly signed — a cabinet blocked by storage or furniture defeats the entire system.






## 5. The fire brigade inlet

A Siamese (twin-headed) inlet at ground level lets the fire brigade pump additional water into the riser from their appliance, boosting pressure and supply beyond what the building's own pumps provide — important for sustained firefighting on upper floors.






## Keeping it ready

A wet riser system is only as good as its last inspection. Weekly pump run-tests, periodic pressure checks, and clear access to every landing valve are the basics — see our fire hydrant maintenance checklist for the full list.

Title: Fire Alarm Panel Faults: Safe First Response for Building Teams
Last updated: 2026-11-01

Samarth Fire Protection System · Technical Guide


# Fire Alarm Panel Faults: Safe First Response for Building Teams

A trouble indication is not proof that there is no fire. It means the building team must identify what the panel is reporting, follow the site procedure and restore the affected system safely.

Published 1 November 2026 · Reviewed for general awareness by Samarth Fire Protection System









## On this page
1. First distinguish an alarm from a trouble condition 2. Safe first-response steps 3. What not to do 4. What to give the technician 5. Confirm restoration before closing the fault 6. Safety and compliance Fire safety FAQs → 
A trouble indication is not proof that there is no fire. It means the building team must identify what the panel is reporting, follow the site procedure and restore the affected system safely.

## First distinguish an alarm from a trouble condition
If there are signs of smoke, heat, burning smell or an activated detector, treat the situation as a possible emergency and follow the building’s evacuation and emergency-response plan. Do not delay an evacuation to investigate the panel. A trouble / fault indication may instead report a wiring, power, battery, device or communication problem—but it still needs prompt attention.



## Safe first-response steps

- Follow the building’s alarm response procedure and check for signs of an actual emergency from a safe location.
- Notify the designated facility manager, security desk or fire-safety coordinator.
- Record the exact panel message, zone, device address and time shown on the panel.
- Keep the panel powered and avoid resets, isolations or bypasses unless the approved procedure and authorised personnel require them.
- Contact the competent fire-alarm service provider and share the recorded information.
- Document any temporary impairment controls required by the building’s approved plan and local direction.



## What not to do

- Do not switch off the panel to stop a buzzer.
- Do not disconnect a detector, battery or circuit just to clear a message.
- Do not repeatedly reset the panel without understanding why the condition occurred.
- Do not assume one faulty zone means the rest of the building is protected.
- Do not use an untrained person to open the panel or modify wiring.



## What to give the technician
Provide the make and model of the panel, displayed message, affected zone or device, time of occurrence, recent maintenance or construction work, any power interruption and whether the issue is intermittent. Ask for a service report that identifies the cause, work performed, parts replaced, remaining impairment (if any), and verification / functional test after repair.



## Confirm restoration before closing the fault
After repair, confirm that the panel is in its normal condition, affected devices and circuits have been tested using the approved method, and any temporary impairment measures have been formally stood down by the responsible person. Update the fault register and inform the relevant building stakeholders.



## Safety and compliance
Site-specific fire-alarm response should follow the approved fire strategy, equipment manuals, applicable standards and directions from the competent fire authority. The Maharashtra Fire & Emergency Services website provides official fire-safety information and circulars.
This is general guidance. It does not replace emergency services, the building’s emergency plan or work by qualified fire-alarm technicians.

Title: Fire Extinguisher Inspection Guide: A Practical Checklist for Buildings
Last updated: 2026-11-01

Samarth Fire Protection System · Technical Guide


# Fire Extinguisher Inspection Guide: A Practical Checklist for Buildings

An extinguisher is useful only when the correct type is available, accessible, in serviceable condition and understood by the people expected to use it. A visual check is not the same as a full service or pressure test.

Published 1 November 2026 · Reviewed for general awareness by Samarth Fire Protection System









## On this page
1. Check whether the extinguisher suits the risk 2. Access and location 3. Visible condition 4. Inspection, servicing and testing 5. Train people without creating extra risk 6. Simple inspection record fields 7. Important note Fire safety FAQs → 
An extinguisher is useful only when the correct type is available, accessible, in serviceable condition and understood by the people expected to use it. A visual check is not the same as a full service or pressure test.

## Check whether the extinguisher suits the risk
Review the hazard and the extinguisher type specified for the location. Different agents are designed for different classes of fire and environments. Do not assume an ABC powder, CO₂, foam or wet-chemical extinguisher is interchangeable. Follow the site fire plan, product label and competent fire-safety advice.



## Access and location

- Confirm the extinguisher is in its designated location and easy to reach.
- Check that cabinets, signs and approach routes are not blocked.
- Confirm the operating instructions and identification labels can be read.
- Check that the extinguisher is mounted or placed as intended by the manufacturer and site plan.



## Visible condition

- Look for corrosion, dents, cracks, leakage or other physical damage.
- Check the pin and tamper seal are present and appear undisturbed.
- Check the hose, horn, nozzle and handle for visible damage or obstruction.
- For units with a pressure gauge, check that the indicator appears in the marked serviceable range.
- Check the inspection / service tag and note any missed or overdue action.
A gauge reading or intact seal alone does not prove an extinguisher is fully serviceable.



## Inspection, servicing and testing
Record the extinguisher ID, location, agent, visual condition, gauge indication where fitted, seal / pin status, tag information, defects and action taken. Follow the applicable edition of the relevant Indian Standard, manufacturer’s instructions and service-provider requirements for maintenance, refilling and hydrostatic testing. The intervals are not identical for every extinguisher type, design or service condition; avoid applying one generic interval to the entire inventory.
Any extinguisher discharged, damaged, leaking, undercharged or otherwise suspect should be removed from service and replaced or serviced under the site’s approved procedure so the area is not left without the planned protection.



## Train people without creating extra risk
Show occupants where extinguishers are located and explain the site’s alarm and evacuation procedure. Only people who have been trained and are confident should consider using a suitable extinguisher on a small, incipient fire when they have a clear escape route. Raise the alarm first; evacuate when conditions are unsafe or the fire is growing. Never encourage occupants to fight a fire instead of leaving.



## Simple inspection record fields
Use a consistent register with columns for extinguisher number, floor / location, type and capacity, accessibility, visible condition, pin / seal, gauge (where fitted), hose / nozzle, service tag, defect, temporary replacement and closure date. Keep the register alongside service certificates and replacement records.



## Important note
Portable fire-extinguisher selection, installation, inspection and maintenance should follow the applicable standard, product instructions and competent advice. For Maharashtra regulatory references, consult the official Fire Acts, Rules and NBC page .
This guide is an awareness checklist, not a substitute for servicing, refilling or hydrostatic testing by a competent service provider.

Title: Fire Hydrant System Maintenance Checklist for Facility Managers
Last updated: 2026-11-01

Samarth Fire Protection System · Technical Guide


# Fire Hydrant System Maintenance Checklist for Facility Managers

A hydrant system is only useful when water supply, pumps, valves, pipework and outlet equipment are available together. A maintenance checklist should therefore cover the complete system and keep a clear record of every inspection and test.

Published 1 November 2026 · Reviewed for general awareness by Samarth Fire Protection System









## On this page
1. Know the system before testing it 2. Visual condition and access 3. Pump room and water supply 4. Pressure and flow are design-specific 5. Set an inspection schedule that can be followed 6. Control impairments and repairs 7. Records to retain 8. Important safety note Fire safety FAQs → 
A hydrant system is only useful when water supply, pumps, valves, pipework and outlet equipment are available together. A maintenance checklist should therefore cover the complete system and keep a clear record of every inspection and test.

## Know the system before testing it
Keep an up-to-date system drawing or asset register showing the pump room, water storage, risers, landing valves, external hydrants, hose reels, isolation valves and control points. Record equipment make, model and identification details where available. Identify which valves must remain in a normal position and who is authorised to operate them.



## Visual condition and access

- Keep hydrant points, hose cabinets, landing valves and pump-room access clear.
- Look for visible leakage, corrosion, physical impact, damaged supports, missing caps or damaged valve handwheels.
- Check that hoses, branch pipes, couplings and nozzles are present, accessible and apparently serviceable.
- Check labels, location signs and operating instructions are legible.
- Report any signs of tampering, unauthorised isolation or missing equipment.



## Pump room and water supply
Review pump controller indications, supply availability, water level records, visible leaks, unusual noise or vibration, battery and fuel readiness for diesel equipment, and the condition of ventilation and drainage. Check that the main, standby and jockey pump arrangements match the approved design and current maintenance instructions.
Functional run tests should be performed only by trained personnel under an approved method. Record the test date, pump identity, starting method, observed readings, abnormalities and corrective work. Do not improvise a test by opening outlets or changing valves without understanding the hydraulic impact.



## Pressure and flow are design-specific
There is no single pressure number that can safely be copied to every building. The required pressure and flow depend on building height, system design, hydraulic calculations, pump duty, outlet location, applicable standards and approved documents. Use calibrated instruments and the defined test points and acceptance criteria for the particular system.



## Set an inspection schedule that can be followed
Use the manufacturer’s instructions, approved maintenance plan, relevant standards, applicable law and the contract with the maintenance provider to set inspection and test intervals. Do not treat this general article as a universal weekly, monthly or annual schedule. Assign an owner for each task and keep missed inspections visible until they are completed.



## Control impairments and repairs
If a pump, tank, riser or outlet is unavailable, record the affected area and duration, notify the building’s responsible manager, and apply the building’s approved impairment / temporary-risk-control procedure. Arrange competent repair and retesting. Do not conceal an impairment or assume an untested repair is service-ready.



## Records to retain

- Asset register and current system drawings.
- Inspection, pump-run, pressure and flow test records.
- Valve status and impairment logs.
- Service reports, replaced parts and calibration details.
- Defect register with closure and retest evidence.
These records also support a building-specific review for statutory maintenance and certification requirements.



## Important safety note
Hydrant testing can create high-pressure water discharge and can affect fire-system readiness. Testing, isolation and reinstatement must be planned and supervised by competent personnel. For State-specific requirements, refer to the Maharashtra Fire & Emergency Services Acts and Rules .

Title: Building Fire Safety Audit Checklist for Owners & Managers
Last updated: 2026-11-01

Samarth Fire Protection System · Technical Guide


# Fire Safety Audit Checklist for Buildings: What Owners and Facility Managers Should Review

A useful fire safety audit does more than count extinguishers. It checks whether the building’s installed protection measures, escape routes, people and maintenance records work together as a practical emergency system.

Published 1 November 2026 · Reviewed for general awareness by Samarth Fire Protection System









## On this page
1. Start with the building and its use 2. 1. Escape routes and means of egress 3. 2. Active fire-protection systems 4. 3. Alarm, detection and communications 5. 4. Housekeeping and ignition risks 6. 5. People, plans and records 7. 6. Turn findings into a corrective-action plan 8. Standards and site-specific requirements Fire safety FAQs → 
A useful fire safety audit does more than count extinguishers. It checks whether the building’s installed protection measures, escape routes, people and maintenance records work together as a practical emergency system.

## Start with the building and its use
Record the building’s occupancy, height, floor count, basements, high-risk rooms, public areas, special hazards and any recent change in use. Review the latest approved fire plans and approvals available to the owner or facility manager. A residential tower, school, hospital, office and industrial premises do not have identical risks or requirements.



## 1. Escape routes and means of egress

- Check that staircases, corridors, exit doors and final discharge routes are not blocked or used for storage.
- Check exit signs and emergency lighting for visible damage and apparent operation.
- Confirm fire doors close properly and are not wedged open or obstructed.
- Check that access to refuge areas and fire-fighting access routes is maintained where applicable.
- Confirm evacuation instructions are visible and understandable to occupants.



## 2. Active fire-protection systems
Review the building’s installed systems rather than assuming every building has the same equipment. Where provided, inspect the visible condition and accessibility of hydrants, landing valves, hose reels, hose boxes, sprinkler controls, fire pumps, water storage, extinguishers, detectors, manual call points and alarm panels.
Check available maintenance records and fault logs. Operational tests should be planned and supervised by competent personnel using the approved procedure so testing does not create an unintended impairment or water release.



## 3. Alarm, detection and communications
Review panel status, recurring faults, disabled or isolated points, detector condition, manual call-point access and any connection to voice or other emergency communication systems. Ask for a documented process to report, investigate and close faults. A panel should not be left switched off simply to silence a trouble indication.



## 4. Housekeeping and ignition risks

- Look for combustible storage in electrical rooms, staircases, corridors and pump rooms.
- Check that electrical panels are accessible and obvious signs of overheating or damaged cables are escalated.
- Review controls for hot work, temporary wiring, waste, gas cylinders and other hazards relevant to the premises.
- Check that fire doors, shafts and service penetrations have not been compromised by later work.



## 5. People, plans and records
Confirm that emergency roles are assigned, staff know how to raise an alarm, evacuation routes and assembly points are known, and assistance arrangements exist for people who may need support. Review induction, drill and contractor briefing records. Make sure current emergency contacts and building plans are accessible to the people who need them.



## 6. Turn findings into a corrective-action plan
For every finding, document the location, evidence, risk level, immediate control, permanent action, owner and due date. Track high-risk items to closure and keep test reports, service records, photographs and retest evidence together. A report that lists defects but never verifies closure is not an effective maintenance process.



## Standards and site-specific requirements
The audit criteria must be based on current applicable legislation, the building’s approved fire strategy, relevant standards, manufacturer instructions and local authority directions. The Maharashtra Fire & Emergency Services resource page provides access to the State’s published fire legislation and rules.
This checklist is an educational starting point, not a statutory audit format and not a replacement for assessment by qualified, appropriately authorised professionals.

Title: Housing Society Fire Drill Guide: Planning a Safer Evacuation
Last updated: 2026-11-01

Samarth Fire Protection System · Technical Guide


# Housing Society Fire Drill Guide: Planning a Safer Evacuation

A fire drill is useful when residents know what the alarm means, where to go and whom to follow. It should be planned for the building’s actual layout and residents—not conducted as a surprise exercise that creates avoidable risk.

Published 1 November 2026 · Reviewed for general awareness by Samarth Fire Protection System









## On this page
1. 1. Plan around the building 2. 2. Assign clear roles 3. 3. Tell residents what to expect 4. 4. Conduct the exercise safely 5. 5. Review the drill and close actions 6. Common mistakes to avoid 7. Local requirements Fire safety FAQs → 
A fire drill is useful when residents know what the alarm means, where to go and whom to follow. It should be planned for the building’s actual layout and residents—not conducted as a surprise exercise that creates avoidable risk.

## 1. Plan around the building
Review the approved evacuation plan, staircase and exit locations, basement routes, refuge areas where applicable, assembly point and access for emergency responders. Identify alternate routes and any areas that may be unavailable during a real incident. Do not invent an escape route that conflicts with the approved plan.



## 2. Assign clear roles

- Appoint a drill coordinator and floor / wing wardens.
- Assign people to raise the alarm, guide movement and report floor status.
- Identify residents, visitors or staff who may need assistance and plan support with their consent.
- Agree how the assembly point will record people and communicate missing-person information to responders.



## 3. Tell residents what to expect
Share the date, time window, alarm signal, route guidance, assembly location and expected behaviour in advance. Provide accessible information for children, older residents, people with disabilities, domestic workers, security teams and visitors. Explain how the drill will be stopped if an actual emergency occurs.



## 4. Conduct the exercise safely

- Use the site’s approved alarm / drill procedure and a coordinator who can stop the exercise.
- Use designated staircases and keep exits, landings and fire-service access routes clear.
- Do not use lifts during evacuation unless the approved emergency plan specifically provides a designated evacuation lift and trained procedure.
- Do not run, push, return for belongings or re-enter until the responsible authority says it is safe.
- Do not use live flames or smoke-producing materials for an ordinary resident drill.
- Do not discharge extinguishers or operate hydrants for demonstration unless the exercise is specifically designed, risk-assessed and supervised by competent trainers.



## 5. Review the drill and close actions
Record the time taken, route bottlenecks, blocked doors, alarm audibility issues, residents who needed assistance, confusion about assembly points and any unsafe behaviour. Assign each improvement to a person with a due date. Share a short summary with residents and repeat the exercise after major changes to the building or emergency plan.



## Common mistakes to avoid

- Announcing an evacuation but not checking if the route is safe.
- Failing to count residents or report people unaccounted for.
- Blocking the assembly point or fire-engine access with parked vehicles.
- Ignoring residents who cannot use stairs independently.
- Treating a drill as a one-off event with no written corrective actions.



## Local requirements
Follow the building’s approved fire and emergency plan, applicable local requirements and instructions from the competent authority. The Maharashtra Fire & Emergency Services publishes official fire-safety resources.
This guide is general resident-awareness material, not a replacement for a site-specific evacuation plan or professional training.
